title: K. MADHUSUDHAN RAO VS. M/S LODHA HEALTHY CONSTRUCTIONS AND DEVELOPER PRIVATE LIMITED (LHCPL)

paras.text:
2026 INSC 1131
1
REPORTABLE
IN THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA
CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION
CIVIL APPEAL NO.8994 OF 2022
MADHU KUDAPA (FORMERLY KNOWN
AS K. MADHUSUDHAN RAO) ...APPELLANT
VERSUS
M/S LODHA HEALTHY CONSTRUCTIONS
AND DEVELOPER PRIVATE LIMITED
(LHCPL) & ANR. ...RESPONDENTS
WITH
CIVIL APPEAL NOS. 4622-4623 OF 2023
JUDGMENT
ALOK ARADHE, J.
1. The purchase of a residential apartment in a project under
construction is, more often than not, financed partly from the
savings of the purchaser and partly by a housing loan, which
the lender disburses directly to the builder under a tripartite
arrangement. When the builder fails to deliver possession
and the purchaser seeks a refund, the question which arises,
is not merely whether the consideration must be returned,
but to whom it must be returned and in what measure.
2. These three appeals preferred under Section 23 of the
Consumer Protection Act, 1986 (the Act) arise out of orders

2
dated 01.07.2022 and 07.12.2022 passed by the National
Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission, New Delhi (the
Commission). Civil Appeal No. 8994 of 2022 has been filed by
the complainant who had booked an apartment, namely, Mr.
K. Madhusudhan Rao (the Borrower), whereas, Civil Appeal
Nos. 4622-4623 of 2023 have been filed by the Housing
Development Finance Corporation Limited (the Bank). In
order to appreciate the grievance of the appellants relevant
facts need mention which are stated infra.
FACTUAL BACKGROUND
3. In the year 2009, M/s Lodha Healthy Constructions and
Developers Private Limited (LHCPL) (the Builder) launched a
residential project called "Lodha Bellezza" at Kukatpally,
Hyderabad. On 08.08.2009, the Borrower, then a Non-resident Indian, booked an apartment for a total
consideration of Rs.2,30,73,876/- (Rupees Two Crore Thirty
Lakh Seventy Three Thousand Eight Hundred Seventy Six
only). The Borrower paid a booking amount of Rs.4,50,000/-
(Rupees Four Lakh Fifty Thousand only). Thereafter, he paid
sums of Rs.22,45,288/- (Rupees Twenty Two Lakh Forty Five
Thousand Two Hundred Eighty Eight only) and 24,16,288/-

3
(Rupees Twenty-Four Lakh Sixteen Thousand Two Hundred
Eighty Eight only) on 25.08.2009 and 30.09.2009
respectively. In all, the Borrower paid a sum of
Rs.51,11,576/- (Rupees Fifty One Lakh Eleven Thousand
Five Hundred Seventy Six only), that is, 22% of the sale
consideration from his own funds. On 21.10.2009, an
Agreement for Sale was executed between the Borrower and
the Builder.
4. In order to make payment of the balance consideration, the
Borrower approached Housing Development Finance
Corporation Limited (the Bank). On 27.11.2009, the Bank
sanctioned a housing loan of Rs.2 Crores. Thereafter, on
30.01.2010, a Tripartite Agreement was executed between
the Borrower, the Builder and the Bank. A Loan Agreement
dated 01.02.2010 was executed between the Bank, the
Borrower and his wife as co-borrower.
5. Between February, 2010 to July, 2011, the Bank disbursed
the sum of Rs.1,68,80,531/- (Rupees One Crore Sixty Eight
Lakh Eighty Thousand Five Hundred Thirty One only) to the
Builder in thirteen tranches. Thus, the Builder received

4
about 95% of the sale consideration from the Borrower as well
as the Bank.
6. Despite having received a substantial amount, there was a
delay in delivery of the possession of the apartment. On
04.08.2011, the Builder informed the Borrower that there
was delay and that possession of the apartment would be
handed over by April, 2012. However, the Builder failed to
deliver the possession even by April, 2012 and between
October and December, 2012 called upon the Borrower to
take the possession for "fit-outs". The Borrower did not
accord his consent to the aforesaid proposal and inquired
whether the Occupancy Certificate and the No-Objection
Certificate (NOC) of the Fire Department had been obtained.
The Builder by communication dated 25.03.2013, informed
the Borrower that NOC of the Fire Department was still
awaited, which according to the Builder was issued in May,
2013.
7. In the meantime, the Bank started debiting pre-EMI interest
on the amount disbursed by it. As per the loan statement
dated 23.03.2013, interest of Rs.41,34,940/- (Rupees Forty
One Lakh Thirty Four Thousand Nine Hundred Forty only)

5
had been debited to the loan account, out of which the
Borrower paid a sum of Rs.26,23,150/- (Rupees Twenty Six
Lakh Twenty Three Thousand One Hundred Fifty only) to the
Bank.
8. On 13.05.2013, the Borrower filed a consumer complaint,
namely, CC No. 150 of 2013, before the Commission seeking
refund of Rs.2,19,92,107/- (Rupees Two Crore Nineteen Lakh
Ninety Two Thousand One Hundred Seven only) with interest
at the rate of 12% per annum compounded quarterly till the
date of the complaint, and interest at the rate of 18% per
annum thereafter, as well as reimbursement of house rent of
Rs.7,97,895/- (Rupees Seven Lakh Ninety Seven Thousand
Eight Hundred Ninety Five only) for the period from
01.07.2011 till 30.04.2013 and further rent thereafter. The
Borrower also prayed for reversal of the interest debited to his
loan account, for a direction that the sum of Rs.26,23,150/-
(Rupees Twenty Six Lakh Twenty Three Thousand One
Hundred Fifty only) collected by the Bank as interest be
treated as repayment towards the principal amount, and for
a sum of Rs.15,00,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Lakh only) as

6
compensation from the Builder and the Bank for mental
trauma, agony and harassment.
9. During the pendency of the complaint, the Bank recalled the
loan by notice dated 19.01.2015 and filed a suit, namely,
COS No. 96 of 2017 before the Commercial Court seeking
recovery of a sum of Rs. 2,51,15,774/- (Rupees Two Crore
Fifty One Lakh Fifteen Thousand Seven Hundred Seventy
Four only) along with interest at the rate of 18% per annum
from the Borrower and his wife. During the pendency of the
complaint as well as the suit, the Borrower paid a further
sum of Rs. 20,00,000/- (Rupees Twenty Lakh only) and
30,00,000/- (Rupees Thirty Lakh only) to the Bank on
23.06.2021 and 14.07.2021 respectively. Thus, the Borrower
in all paid Rs. 76,23,150/- (Rupees Seventy Six Lakh Twenty
Three Thousand One Hundred Fifty only) to the Bank.
THE ORDER OF THE COMMISSION
10. The Commission by its order dated 01.07.2022, inter alia held
that the Borrower is a consumer and that there was a delay
in delivery of possession of the apartment, for which the
Borrower is entitled to refund of the principal amount along
with reasonable interest. The Commission rejected the plea

7
of force majeure raised by the Builder, holding that the
Builder had merely narrated events and obstacles routinely
faced by developers, had not intimated the Borrower of any
force majeure condition at the relevant time, and had failed
to show that the occupancy certificate had been received. The
Commission noticed that under Recital (H) of the tripartite
agreement and Clause 2.4 of the Loan Agreement, the Bank
was to disburse the loan after verifying the progress of
construction. The Commission held that the Bank did not
adduce any evidence of such verification, found the Bank to
be deficient in service, and directed the Bank to pay a sum of
Rs.2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lakh only) to the Borrower. The
Commission further directed the Builder to refund the entire
amount deposited by the Borrower with interest at the rate of
9% per annum from the date of the respective deposits till
realisation within a period of three months, failing which the
Builder was to pay the principal amount with interest at the
rate of 12% per annum. The Commission, however, did not
advert to the claim of the Borrower for reimbursement of
house rent and for compensation.

8
11. Being aggrieved by the direction of the Commission to refund
the entire amount to the Borrower, the Bank preferred a
review petition which was dismissed vide order dated
07.12.2022 by the Commission.
12. The Builder did not challenge the order of the Commission
and sought leave to deposit the amount due under it. On
01.02.2023, the Commission permitted the Builder to deposit
a sum of Rs.4,43,24,510/- (Rupees Four Crore Forty Three
Lakh Twenty Four Thousand Five Hundred Ten only) without
prejudice to the rights and contentions of the parties. The
said amount was deposited by the Builder. The amount so
deposited, together with the interest accrued thereon, stood
at Rs.5,65,43,411/- (Rupees Five Crore Sixty Five Lakh Forty
Three Thousand Four Hundred Eleven only) as on
08.10.2026.
13. On 10.12.2024, the Commercial Court dismissed the suit
filed by the Bank on the ground that in view of findings
recorded by the Commission in Consumer Complaint, the
suit was not maintainable. However, the Commercial Court
did not answer the remaining issues in the suit. Being

9
aggrieved, the Bank has filed an appeal which is pending
before the High Court.
14. By an order dated 07.11.2025, this Court declined to grant
interim relief to the Bank, but directed that the disbursal of
the amounts would be subject to the final outcome of the
appeals. By a subsequent order dated 22.05.2026, this Court
permitted the Borrower to withdraw 50% of the amount
deposited by the Builder before the Commission on
furnishing a bank guarantee to the satisfaction of the
Commission.
15. Being aggrieved by the denial of the claim for house rent and
compensation, and by the rate of interest, the Borrower has
filed the Civil Appeal No. 8994 of 2022. Being aggrieved by
the finding recorded by the Commission with regard to
deficiency of service on the part of the Bank and the
consequential direction to pay a sum of Rs. 2,00,000/-
(Rupees Two Lakh only) as well as the direction to refund the
entire amount along with interest to the Borrower, the Bank
has filed the Civil Appeal Nos. 4622-4623. The Bank has also
challenged the order dated 07.12.2022 by which its review
petition was rejected.

10
SUBMISSIONS
16. Mr. Amit Anand Tiwari, learned senior counsel for the
Borrower, submitted that the loan was to be disbursed as per
the schedule and in step with the construction and the Bank
while disbursing the amount of loan failed to adhere to the
schedule. It was contended that about 80% of the amount
was disbursed at a time when the Builder did not even have
permission to construct and the project was joint venture of
the Bank and the Builder and they have acted in collusion. It
was urged that the Borrower was entitled to rent for a period
from 30.06.2011 to 01.07.2022 as well as compensation and
the aforesaid prayers of the Borrower were not even adverted
to by the Commission. It was also urged that the Borrower is
entitled to 18% interest on the amount due to him. It was
argued that the Borrower is entitled to refund of the entire
amount including the amount paid by the Bank on his behalf
and he shall pay the amount to the Bank in case the Bank
succeeds in its appeal pending before the High Court. It was
urged that the appeal filed by the Bank is barred by res
judicata as the suit filed by the Bank was dismissed. Our
attention was also invited to the averments in the rejoinder

11
affidavit filed by the Borrower before this Court wherein a
claim had been made for payment of rent at the rate of Rs.
38000/- (Rupees Thirty Eight Thousand only) per month
from July 2011 to July 2013 and at the rate of Rs. 65000/-
(Rupees Sixty Five Thousand only) per month from August
2013 to October 2022. It was also pointed out that the
Borrower had incurred litigation expenses of Rs. 35,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty Five Lakh only) and the Borrower was entitled
to the payment of said amounts. In support of the aforesaid
submissions, reliance has been placed on a decision of this
Court1
.
17. Mr. Gaurav Agarwal, learned senior counsel and Mr. Rahul
Kripalani learned counsel for the Builder, submitted that
Builder has accepted the order passed by the Commission
and with a view to bring quietus to the dispute has submitted
that out of the amount deposited by the Builder, the amount
of Rs.1.27 Crores which was paid by the Borrower from his
own pocket be refunded to the Borrower along with such rate
of interest, as this Court may deem fit. It was further
submitted that the remaining amount with interest accrued
1 Rajnesh Sharma v. Business Park Town Planners Ltd., 2025 SCC OnLine SC 2061

12
thereon be paid to the Bank so that the present appeals as
well as the first appeal filed by the Bank pending before the
High Court can be disposed of. Alternatively, learned senior
counsel has supported the order passed by the Commission
and has submitted that the Borrower is entitled to 9%
interest which has rightly been awarded to him. It was
pointed out that the Borrower in his letter dated 03.11.2012
had himself quantified the loss in terms of rent which the
apartment could have fetched, and the Borrower stands
adequately compensated by the award of interest. In support
of the aforesaid submissions, reliance has been placed on the
decisions of this Court2
.
18. Ms. Suhasini Sen, learned counsel for the Bank, submitted
that the Commission erred in granting refund of the entire
amount of Rs.2.19 Crores to the Borrower in violation of
Clauses 16 and 17 of the Tripartite Agreement. It was
contended that by cancellation of allotment, the Bank which
was a secured creditor had been reduced to the position of an
unsecured creditor. It was urged that the finding recorded by
the Commission that there was deficiency on the part of the
2 Experion Developers (P) Ltd. v. Sushma Ashok Shiroor, (2022) 15 SCC 286 and DLF Homes Panchkula
(P) Ltd. v. D.S. Dhanda, (2020) 16 SCC 318

13
Bank cannot be sustained on the basis of material placed on
record. However, it was submitted that the proposal made by
the Builder for amicable settlement of dispute was not
acceptable to the Bank. It was contended that the suit was
dismissed solely on the ground of maintainability and there
had been no adjudication on merits and an appeal against
the said judgment of the Commercial Court is pending,
therefore, the doctrine of res judicata has no application.
Lastly, it was contended that the rights of the Bank to recover
the amount from the Borrower cannot be adjudicated in a
complaint filed by a consumer.
ISSUES
19. We have considered the rival submissions and have perused
the record.
20. The issues which arise for consideration are as follows:-
(a) whether the Borrower is entitled to refund of the entire
amount including the amount disbursed by the Bank, and if
so, at what rate of interest?
(b) whether the Borrower is entitled to compensation,
including reimbursement of the rent claimed by him?

14
(c) whether the Bank was deficient in rendering service to
the Borrower?
(d) the relief to which the Bank is entitled to in these
proceedings.
21. Now, we proceed to deal with the issues ad seriatim.
ANALYSIS
(a) WHETHER THE BORROWER IS ENTITLED TO REFUND
OF THE ENTIRE AMOUNT INCLUDING THE AMOUNT
DEPOSITED BY THE BANK, IF SO, AT WHAT RATE OF
INTEREST?
22. The entitlement of the Borrower to refund of the entire
amount is required to be examined on the touchstone of the
principle that no one shall be enriched at the expense of
another. The principle is of ancient origin and finds
expression in the maxim nemo debet locupletari ex aliena
jactura, that is, no one ought to be enriched by the loss of
another.
23. In India, the principle has a statutory home. Chapter V of the
Indian Contract Act, 1872 (the Contract Act), comprising
Sections 68 to 72, deals with "certain relations resembling
those created by contract". Section 70 of the Contract Act
obliges a person who enjoys the benefit of a lawful, non-gratuitous act of another to compensate him. Section 72

15
mandates that a person to whom money has been paid, or
anything delivered, by mistake or under coercion, must repay
or return it. Sections 64 and 65 require a benefit received
under a contract which is rescinded, or which becomes void,
to be restored to the person from whom it was received.
24. The elements of the Doctrine of Unjust Enrichment were
identified by this Court in Mahabir Kishore v. State of
Madhya Pradesh3
, and it was held that the doctrine
proceeds on the basis that it would be unjust to allow one
person to retain a benefit received at the expense of another.
Stated simply, 'unjust enrichment' means retention of a
benefit by a person that is unjust or inequitable4
. It has also
been described as "the unjust retention of a benefit to the loss
of another"5
. A Bench of nine Judges of this Court applied the
doctrine to claims for refund of duties and held that a
claimant who has passed on the burden of a duty to others
cannot recover it for himself, for he has suffered no loss6
.
25. Three things follow. First, the doctrine is part of our law, both
by statute and as a principle of equity. Second, it looks at the
3
(1989) 4 SCC 1
4 Sahakari Khand Udyog Mandal Ltd. v. Commissioner of Central Excise, (2005) 3 SCC 738
5
Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action v. Union of India, (2011) 8 SCC 161
6 Mafatlal Industries Ltd. v. Union of India, (1997) 5 SCC 536

16
person who holds a benefit and asks whether, in conscience,
he may keep it. Third, it is a doctrine of correction and not of
reward. Restitution restores. It does not redistribute. It
returns value to the person at whose expense it was received.
It does not confer value on a person merely because he has
been wronged.
26. The law of contract compensates, it does not enrich. Even
while enhancing the rate of interest payable to a buyer, this
Court in Rajnesh Sharma (supra) cautioned that the
objective of granting compensation cannot be altered such
that it amounts to a windfall gain to the other party.
27. In the backdrop of the aforesaid well-settled legal principles,
we advert to the facts of the case in hand. The transaction is
triangular. The Builder received Rs.2,19,92,107/- (Rupees
Two Crore Nineteen Lakh Ninety Two Thousand One Hundred
Seven only) and gave nothing in return. The retention of that
amount by the Builder is plainly unjust, and the Builder has
rightly not disputed its liability to refund it. The real question
is to whom the refund must go. The money came from two
sources. Admittedly, the Borrower paid a sum of
Rs.51,11,576/- (Rupees Fifty One Lakh Eleven Thousand

17
Five Hundred Seventy Six only) to the Builder from his own
funds. He also paid a sum of Rs.76,23,150/- (Rupees Seventy
Six Lakh Twenty Three Thousand One Hundred Fifty only) to
the Bank, comprising Rs.26,23,150/- (Rupees Twenty Six
Lakh Twenty Three Thousand One Hundred Fifty only) paid
towards interest up to March, 2013, Rs.20,00,000/- (Rupees
Twenty Lakh only) paid on 23.06.2021 and Rs.30,00,000/-
(Rupees Thirty Lakh only) paid on 14.07.2021. Thus, the
Borrower paid a total sum of Rs.1,27,34,726/- (Rupees One
Crore Twenty Seven Lakh Thirty Four Thousand Seven
Hundred Twenty Six only) out of his own pocket. The
remaining amount was paid by the Bank to the Builder out
of the loan, and has not been repaid by the Borrower.
28. It is true that under Recital (H) and Clause 4 of the Tripartite
Agreement, a disbursal to the Builder is deemed to be a
disbursal to the Borrower. That fiction, however, serves a
limited purpose. It fastens the obligation to repay the loan on
the Borrower, though the money never passed through his
hands. It does not convert borrowed money, which remains
unpaid, into the Borrower's own money. The Commission
nevertheless directed refund of Rs.2,19,92,107/- (Rupees

18
Two Crore Nineteen Lakh Ninety Two Thousand One Hundred
Seven only) to the Borrower along with interest, without any
reference to the lender whose money it largely was. Payment
of the entire amount to the Borrower, while the loan remains
outstanding and the claim of the Bank is in dispute, would
place in his hands a sum which he has not paid. It amounts
to unjust enrichment, which is impermissible in law. We,
therefore, hold that the Borrower is entitled, in his own right,
to refund of a sum of Rs.1,27,34,726/- (Rupees One Crore
Twenty Seven Lakh Thirty Four Thousand Seven Hundred
Twenty Six only).
29. Now we examine the claim of the Borrower for interest. The
relevant extract of Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale dated
21.10.2009 reads as under: -
"24. The Builder/Promoter shall give
possession of the said Residential
Apartment to the purchaser on or before
30th day of June, 2011. The
Builder/Promoter shall be entitled to a
grace period of 6 months if he fails or
neglects to give possession of the said
Residential Apartment to the Purchaser on
or before the date aforesaid on account of
reasons beyond its control. In the event,
the Builder/Promoter fails to handover the
possession of the Residential Apartment to
the Purchaser beyond the said grace period

19
of 6 months, then and in that event, the
Builder/Promoter shall, on demand, be
liable to refund to the Purchaser the
compensation calculated at the rate of 12
percent per annum on the amounts paid
by the Purchaser from the date of expiry of
such grace period of 6 months ...
Alternatively, on such expiry of the said
grace period of 6 months, the Purchaser
may by giving notice in writing to the
builder elect to terminate this Agreement
and in such event, the Builder/Promoter
shall on demand be liable to refund to the
Purchaser the amounts already received
by the Builder/Promoter in respect of the
said premises with simple interest at 12
percent per annum from the date the
Builder/Promoter received such demand
till the date of refund. ..."
30. Thus, by Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale, the parties
themselves have fixed the rate of interest at 12% per annum.
Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale provides that the Builder
must pay compensation at the rate of 12% per annum in case
it fails to deliver the apartment in time, and that in case the
purchaser terminates the agreement, the Builder must
refund the amount to the purchaser with simple interest at
the rate of 12% per annum. The Borrower himself, in his
complaint, claimed interest at the rate of 12% per annum up
to the date of the complaint. The claim of the Borrower for
interest at the rate of 18% per annum, founded on Clause 19

20
of the Agreement for Sale and on the decision in Rajnesh
Sharma (supra), is of no assistance to him. Clause 19 does
not stand alone; Clause 24 stands beside it and specifically
governs the consequence of the Builder's default. In Rajnesh
Sharma (supra), this Court enhanced the rate of interest
from 9% to 18% in view of the conduct of the builder, who
had kept the buyer waiting for over a decade and had charged
him interest at 18% for delayed payments. This Court,
however, made it clear that what is reasonable varies from
case to case, and that the rate of interest charged by the
builder cannot be granted to the buyer as a rule of thumb.
This Court has also held that interest at 18% cannot be
awarded as a uniform rule, and that the relief must depend
on the facts of each case7
. Where the parties have agreed
upon a particular consequence of delay in handing over
possession, require strong reasons to depart from it8
.
31. For the aforementioned reasons, and especially in view of
Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale, the Borrower is entitled
7 Ghaziabad Development Authority v. Balbir Singh, (2004) 5 SCC 65
8 DLF Homes Panchkula Pvt. Ltd. v. D.S. Dhanda, (2020) 16 SCC 318 and Greater Mohali Area
Development Authority v. Anupam Garg, 2025 SCC OnLine SC 1312

21
to simple interest at the rate of 12% per annum. The interest
shall run from the date of each payment.
32. Accordingly, issue (a) is answered by stating that the
Borrower is entitled to refund of a sum of Rs. 1,27,34,726/-
(Rupees One Crore Twenty Seven Lakh Thirty Four Thousand
Seven Hundred Twenty Six only), that is the amount
deposited by him along with interest at the rate of 12% per
annum from the date of each deposit till the amount is paid
to the Borrower.
(b) WHETHER THE BORROWER IS ENTITLED TO
COMPENSATION, INCLUDING REIMBURSEMENT OF THE
RENT CLAIMED BY HIM?
33. The complaint made by the Borrower was not confined to
refund of the amount and interest. The Borrower had sought
reimbursement of rent of Rs.7,97,895/- (Rupees Seven Lakh
Ninety Seven Thousand Eight Hundred Ninety Five only) for
the period from 01.07.2011 to 30.04.2013 and further rent
thereafter, and had also claimed a sum of Rs.15,00,000/-
(Rupees Fifteen Lakh only) for mental agony and harassment.
The Commission reproduced these prayers in its order and
even observed that the Borrower was entitled to refund of the
amount deposited along with compensation. Yet, the

22
operative part of its order grants no compensation against the
Builder. The prayers were not adverted to at all. The grievance
of the Borrower in this regard is, to that extent, well founded.
34. The power to award compensation flows from Section 14(1)(d)
read with Section 22 of the Act. In Lucknow Development
Authority v. M.K. Gupta9
, this Court explained that the Act
enables the consumer to claim, and the forum to award, not
only the value of the goods or services but also compensation
for the injustice suffered. In Ghaziabad Development
Authority (supra), this Court held that what is awarded
under the Act is compensation, that is, a recompense for the
loss or injury, and that it "necessarily has to be based on a
finding of loss or injury and has to correlate with the amount
of loss or injury". The Court illustrated that where possession
is not given, the loss may be determined on the basis of the
rent which could have been earned, or the rent actually paid
by the consumer. In Bangalore Development Authority v.
Syndicate Bank10, this Court held that where possession is
not delivered within the stipulated time, the allottee is
entitled to refund of the amount paid with reasonable interest
9
(1994) 1 SCC 243
10 (2007) 6 SCC 711

23
from the date of payment, and may in addition be entitled to
compensation, as may be decided with reference to the facts
of each case. The power, however, is to award compensation
for loss or injury suffered by the consumer due to the
negligence of the opposite party. It is a power to compensate
for a loss which is proved and which flows from the default.
It is not a power to award every expense which the consumer
has incurred during the pendency of the dispute. Damages
for contractual breach are generally compensatory; an award
which surpasses actual loss enters the domain of a gain-based remedy, and the court must take a balanced approach
so as to ensure right compensation.11
35. Before this Court, the claim for rent has grown far beyond
what was initially claimed before the Commission. In the
rejoinder affidavit, for the first time, the rent at Rs.38,000/-
(Rupees Thirty Eight Thousand only) per month from July,
2011 to July, 2013, and the rent at Rs.65,000/- (Rupees
Sixty Five Thousand only) per month from August, 2013 to
October, 2022 has been claimed. The aforesaid sum cannot
be permitted to be claimed for the first time in these Civil
11 Fortune Infrastructure v. Trevor D'lima, (2018) 5 SCC 442

24
Appeals. For the reasons which follow, we are not persuaded
to compensate the Borrower for the rent so claimed.
36. Firstly, the Act has no provision corresponding to provisions
in other branches of law, such as Rent Control legislations
which statutorily recognises the right of a tenant to claim
rent, in case he hands over the possession of the tenanted
premises for reconstruction/rebuilding.
37. Secondly, the award of rent in addition to interest on the full
refund would amount to double compensation for the same
default. Interest at 12% per annum is awarded precisely
because the Borrower was deprived of the use of his money.
Had that money been with him, he could have applied it to
secure a home of his own. In D.S. Dhanda (supra), this
Court, relying on Irrigation Department, Government of
Orissa v. G.C. Roy,12, held that a person deprived of the use
of money to which he is legitimately entitled has a right to be
compensated for that deprivation, which may be called
interest, compensation or damages; that "such interest will
take into its ambit, the consequences of delay in not handing
over his possession"; and that an award "under various heads
12 (1992) 1 SCC 508

25
in respect of the same default is not sustainable". The Court
further held that the consumer fora "cannot award interest
and/or compensation by applying rule of thumb". To award
him both, the return on the money which would have bought
him a home and the rent which he paid for want of one would
be to compensate him twice for the same loss.
38. Thirdly, the claim travels beyond the pleadings and the proof.
The complaint quantified the rent at Rs.7,97,895/- (Rupees
Seven Lakh Ninety Seven Thousand Eight Hundred Ninety
Five only) for the period up to 30.04.2013. The figures for the
subsequent period, running into several lakhs every year, are
stated for the first time in a rejoinder affidavit in this Court,
supported only by a bank statement for the year 2021. No
lease deed, rent receipt or other evidence of the tenancy was
placed before the Commission. A claim of this magnitude
cannot be adjudicated in a statutory appeal on the strength
of averments made in a rejoinder.
39. Fourthly, and more fundamentally, the Borrower elected his
remedy. Clause 24 of the Agreement for Sale provides two
alternative remedies upon the Builder's failure to deliver
possession. The purchaser may stay in the project and

26
receive compensation at the rate of 12% per annum till
possession is handed over; or he may terminate the
agreement and receive a refund of the amount paid with
simple interest at the rate of 12% per annum. By filing the
complaint on 13.05.2013 and seeking a refund, the Borrower
chose the second course. Having chosen to give up the
apartment, he cannot claim, in addition, the rent which he
would have saved had he taken possession of it. From the
date of that election, the cost of housing himself is not a loss
caused by the non-delivery of an apartment which he no
longer wished to have. It is a cost which every person must
bear, whether he owns a home or rents one. The obligation of
the Builder thereafter was to return his money with interest,
and that obligation is being enforced.
40. Lastly, the claim is inconsistent with the Borrower's own
case. By his letter dated 03.11.2012, the Borrower quantified
his loss as the rent which he could have earned by letting out
the apartment, at about Rs.1,50,000/- (Rupees One Lakh
Fifty Thousand only) per month. The same apartment, for the
same period, cannot be the source both of rent which the
Borrower would have received and of rent which he was

27
compelled to pay. Further, the Borrower has stated that he
resided in rented premises until he purchased another
apartment. Under Section 73 of the Contract Act,
compensation is payable for loss which naturally arose in the
usual course of things from the breach, and, by the
Explanation to that Section, the means which existed of
remedying the inconvenience caused by the non-performance
must be taken into account. A purchaser who has elected to
take his money back, and who has the benefit of interest on
it, cannot claim rent indefinitely thereafter.
41. The claim of compensation quantified by the Borrower
himself in the consumer complaint filed on 13.05.2013 was
Rs. 7,97,895/- (Rupees Seven Lakh Ninety Seven Thousand
Eight Hundred Ninety Five only). The Borrower has been
subjected to prolonged uncertainty, having paid about 95%
of the consideration by July 2011 and having been kept out
of both the apartment and his money for over fifteen years.
The Borrower has been deprived of the benefit of escalation
in the price of the apartment and therefore, compensation, in
such a case has to be higher than the return of the money
deposited by the Borrower. The quantum of compensation

28
depends on the facts of each case. Having regard to the
totality of circumstances and in order to avoid prolonged
inquiry, at this distance of time, we deem it appropriate to
award a sum of Rs. 15,00,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Lakh only)
to the Borrower as compensation. The said amount shall be
towards full and final satisfaction of all the claims of the
Borrower against the Builder towards rent, mental agony,
harassment and litigation expenses. Issue (b) is answered
accordingly.
(c) WHETHER THE BANK WAS DEFICIENT IN RENDERING
SERVICE TO THE BORROWER?
42. Section 2(1)(g) of the Act defines "deficiency" as any fault,
imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality,
nature and manner of performance which is required to be
maintained under any law, or which has been undertaken to
be performed in pursuance of a contract or otherwise, in
relation to any service. Deficiency is a matter of proof. The
burden of proving it lies on the person who alleges it13
. This
Court has reiterated that the initial burden of proving
deficiency in service is on the complainant, and that the
13 Ravneet Singh Bagga v. KLM Royal Dutch Airlines, (2000) 1 SCC 66

29
burden shifts to the opposite party only when that initial
burden is discharged.
14
43. The Borrower discharged his initial burden. He repeatedly
asked the Bank to verify the progress of construction. By e-mail dated 21.03.2010, he sought the Bank's own
assessment of the construction activity. On 24.05.2011, he
told the Builder that the progress made did not justify further
payment; yet the last tranche was released in July, 2011. By
a letter dated 22.06.2012 and e-mails dated 29.10.2012 and
30.10.2012, he sought its inspection reports and an
inspection by a third party. By 30.06.2011, when possession
was due, the Builder had received about 95% of the
consideration. Yet on 30.10.2012 the Bank itself reported the
building to be only 90% ready, and the fire no-objection
certificate came to be issued only in May, 2013. The burden
then shifted to the Bank. Whether it verified the progress of
construction before each disbursal was a fact especially
within its knowledge. Although the Bank claimed, by its reply
dated 02.05.2012, that its engineers had inspected the site
before each release, it produced no inspection report before
14 SGS (India) Ltd. v. Dolphin International Ltd., (2022) 19 SCC 442

30
the Commission. Its written version was not taken on record,
and it led no evidence. Its witness in the suit stated that such
reports were not required. The fact that the thirteen tranches
matched the stage-wise instalments in Clause 6 of the
Agreement for Sale, or that the Borrower forwarded the
Builder's demands, indicates only that the Bank paid what
was demanded. It does not show that the Bank verified the
stage of construction, as its own letter of sanction obliged it
to do.
44. The finding of deficiency recorded by the Commission is thus
a finding of fact founded on the material on record. It is
neither perverse nor based on no evidence. The compensation
of Rs.2,00,000/- (Rupees Two Lakh only) awarded against the
Bank is modest and commensurate with the deficiency. We
find no ground to interfere with it, either at the instance of
the Bank or at the instance of the Borrower. The finding of
deficiency and the direction to the Bank to pay Rs.2,00,000/-
(Rupees Two Lakh only) to the Borrower are accordingly
upheld. Accordingly, issue (c) is answered.
(d) THE RELIEF TO WHICH THE BANK IS ENTITLED TO
IN THESE PROCEEDINGS

31
45. These proceedings arise out of consumer complaint in which
the claim of the Bank based on tripartite agreement cannot
be examined. The Bank is entitled to recover the sum lawfully
due to it from the Borrower. It is noteworthy that the Bank
has already initiated proceedings for recovery of the amount
due to it by filing a suit before the Commercial Court, which
was dismissed, and its claim is now pending in appeal before
the High Court. We, therefore, cannot examine the claim of
the Bank in these proceedings; it is required to be adjudicated
in the appeal pending before the High Court. The High Court
shall decide the appeal on its own merits. All contentions of
the Bank and the Borrower, including the contention of the
Borrower regarding his liability under the loan, are left open.
46. Now, we deal with I.A. No. 95385 of 2026, by which Borrower
seeks amendment of the cause title and the memo of parties.
The Borrower not only seeks change of his name but also
seeks to bring on record the present names of the
respondents. The description of the respondents as proposed
by the Borrower has been opposed by the respondents. We
are, therefore, not inclined to permit to change the
description of respondents. However, from the document

32
annexed with the application, we are satisfied that the name
of the appellant has been changed from K. Madhusudhan
Rao to Madhu Kudapa. The application is, therefore, allowed
to the limited extent of permitting the Borrower to change his
name in the cause title and the memo of parties. Accordingly,
I.A. No. 95385 of 2026 is disposed of.
CONCLUSION AND DIRECTIONS
47. For the foregoing reasons, the following directions are
issued:-

Rs.1,27,34,726/- (Rupees One Crore Twenty Seven

only) along with interest at the rate of 12% per annum
from the date of respective deposits made by the
Borrower to the Builder and the Bank till the date of
payment.
(ii) The Commission shall release a further sum of
Rs.15,00,000/- (Rupees Fifteen Lakh only) to the
Borrower as compensation out of the said deposit,
within a period of one month from today.

33
(iii) The remaining amount shall be kept by the Commission
in an interest bearing account which shall abide by the
decision of the appeal filed by the Bank.
(iv) The High Court shall decide the appeal pending before
it without being influenced by any of the observations
made herein, on its own merits.
48. The order of the Commission is modified accordingly. The
Appeals are disposed of accordingly. There shall be no order
